about: Daily lessons for Laro's Academy: general UK commercial property knowledge, nothing private.

lessons.sub: When a tenant wants to hand the lease on
lessons.why: Tenants selling a business almost always want to assign the lease. Landlords then ask who will stand behind the new tenant. Knowing how an assignment works lets you keep a sale of a business, or an investment sale, moving.
points: Assignment transfers the whole lease to a new tenant for the rest of the term; subletting creates a new, shorter lease underneath it.
Most leases need the landlord's consent to assign, which can't be unreasonably withheld, but the lease can list conditions the landlord may impose.
For leases granted since 1996, the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995 releases the outgoing tenant on assignment, unless it signs an authorised guarantee agreement (AGA).
An AGA makes the outgoing tenant guarantee the incoming tenant only: once that tenant assigns again, the AGA falls away.
The landlord's consent comes in a licence to assign, often with a new rent deposit deed and a guarantor for the incoming tenant.
On an investment sale, the buyer's solicitor will ask for every licence, AGA and deposit deed, so collect them early.
say: "The landlord will consent, but they'll want the current tenant to sign an AGA, so they stand behind the new tenant until it hands the lease on."
"Have you got the licence to assign and the deposit deed from when the lease was last passed on? The buyer's solicitor will want them."
ask: Is the lease being assigned with the business, or will the new tenant take a new lease?
Will the outgoing tenant sign an AGA?
Is there a rent deposit, and will it move across to the new tenant?
cards: Assignment or subletting: which transfers the whole lease?
Assignment. Subletting creates a new lease underneath.
What does an AGA do?
The outgoing tenant guarantees the incoming tenant's obligations.
Does an AGA cover the next tenant after that?
No: only the immediate assignee.
Which Act releases tenants on assignment for leases granted since 1996?
The Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995.
What document gives the landlord's consent to assign?
A licence to assign.

lessons.sub: Why a tenant's break can fail on a technicality
lessons.why: A break clause lets a tenant end a lease early, so it shapes what a tenant will pay and what an investor will pay. Breaks fail on small slips, and a failed break leaves the tenant on the hook for years. Knowing the traps lets you warn clients early and keep deals honest.
points: Courts apply strict compliance: every condition must be met exactly as the lease says, and near enough is not good enough.
Time is of the essence: a break notice served even one day late is ineffective, so check the notice period, form and method of service in the lease itself.

Typical conditions are serving notice, paying rent and other sums due up to the break date, and giving vacant possession; even a small rent shortfall was fatal in Avocet v Merol (2011), so pay every sum demanded and argue afterwards.
Vacant possession means leaving nothing behind: in NYK Logistics v Ibrend Estates (2011) old racking left in the unit defeated the break.

In Marks and Spencer v BNP Paribas (2015) the Supreme Court refused to imply a refund of rent paid in advance for the period after the break date, so a tenant needs an express apportionment clause or a break date on the last day of a rent quarter.

Wording matters: "no breach" conditions are risky because most leases carry minor breaches, while "material compliance" allows minor ones; the RICS leasing code recommends limiting conditions to paying the main rent and giving up occupation.
say: "Before you serve the break notice, let's get your solicitor to list every condition, because the courts won't forgive even a small slip."
"If your break date falls mid-quarter, you may pay the whole quarter and not get any of it back unless the lease says so, so let's push for a refund clause now."
ask: "When is the break date, and how much notice does the lease need?"
"What conditions are attached: rent paid, vacant possession, no breaches?"
"Does the lease refund rent paid in advance for the time after the break?"
"What will be left in the unit, such as racking, partitions or fit-out?"
cards: How strictly do courts read break conditions?
Strictly: every condition must be met exactly; near compliance fails.
What happens to a break notice served one day late?
It is ineffective, because time is of the essence.
What defeated the break in NYK Logistics v Ibrend?
Old racking left in the unit meant no vacant possession.
What did the Supreme Court decide in M&S v BNP Paribas (2015)?
No implied refund of rent paid in advance for the period after the break; it needs an express clause.
What break conditions does the RICS leasing code recommend?
Only paying the main rent and giving up occupation.

lessons.t: Net initial yield and buyer's costs
lessons.sub: Why the yield an investor quotes is lower than rent over price
lessons.why: Investors price shops, offices and units by yield, and they work it out on the full cost of buying, not just the price. If you quote rent divided by price, your yield looks better than the buyer's own sums and you lose credibility. Knowing how buyer's costs move the figure helps you set asking prices and handle offers.
points: Net initial yield (NIY) is a property's net annual income as a percentage of the full cost of buying it: net income divided by (price plus buyer's costs), times 100.
Buyer's costs usually include the purchase tax, agent and legal fees, and VAT on those fees; in England the purchase tax is Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT), while Wales and Scotland have their own taxes.
For a non-residential freehold in England, SDLT is 0% up to £150,000, 2% on the portion from £150,001 to £250,000, and 5% above £250,000; so £275,000 pays £3,250 and £400,000 pays £9,500.
A worked example: £65,000 net income on a £1,000,000 price is 6.5% on price alone, but with about £60,000 of buyer's costs the NIY is £65,000 divided by £1,060,000, or 6.1%.
Turn it round to price a deal: capital value is income divided by the yield; an office let at £70,000 a year at an 8% yield is worth about £875,000 before allowing for costs.
Gross yield is rent over cost with nothing deducted; yields generally fall when the market is buoyant and rise when it is falling, so a lower yield means a higher price.
say: "At that price it shows about 6.5% on the rent, and nearer 6.1% once a buyer adds stamp duty and fees, so that's the figure investors will compare it on."
"If you want a buyer to see a 7% net initial yield, we have to price it net of their costs, not just rent over price."
ask: "What net yield are you looking to achieve after your costs?"
"Is the rent you've quoted the net income, or are there costs the landlord pays out of it?"
"Are you buying in your own name, a company or a pension scheme, and will VAT be charged on the price?"
"Have your solicitor and lender given you a figure for fees, so we can work out your all-in cost?"
cards: What is the formula for net initial yield?
Net annual income divided by (price plus buyer's costs), times 100.
What do buyer's costs usually include?
The purchase tax (SDLT in England), agent and legal fees, and VAT on those fees.
What are the non-residential SDLT bands in England?
£65,000 income, £1,000,000 price, £60,000 costs: what NIY?
6.1% (6.5% on price alone).
An office let at £70,000 a year at an 8% yield is worth about?
£875,000: income divided by the yield.

lessons.t: A small unit enquiry, step by step
lessons.sub: A made-up call about a workshop unit, where business rates relief decides the deal
lessons.why: Small occupiers often judge a unit on rent alone and get a shock when the rates bill arrives. If you can explain small business rate relief on the first call, you qualify them properly and stop deals falling over later. This made-up scenario shows what to ask and say at each step.
points: The call (made up): a sole trader runs a van repair business from a unit in Fenton and rings about a 1,200 sq ft workshop in Longton, asking rent £7,800 a year, rateable value £6,500. First find out why they are moving and when, before talking price.
Ask early whether they will keep their current unit. Small business rate relief is for a business that uses only one property, so a second unit changes the sums.

On GOV.UK, a business using one property with a rateable value of £12,000 or less pays no business rates. From £12,001 to £15,000 the relief goes down gradually from 100% to 0%: £13,500 gets 50% off and £14,000 gets 33% off.

If they take a second property, relief on the main property continues for 36 months where the second property was taken on or after 27 November 2025 (12 months if before). After that it continues only if no other property has a rateable value above £2,899 and the total of all of them is under £20,000 (£28,000 in London).

Relief is not automatic in practice: the occupier contacts the local council to check eligibility and get it, and must tell the council when circumstances change, such as taking another property. For 2026/27 the standard multiplier is 48p and the small business multiplier is 43.2p, for rateable values below £51,000.

Close for the next step, not the deal: book a viewing, and agree the main terms you will put in heads of terms (rent, length of lease, any break, deposit or guarantee, repairs, use and whether the lease is inside or outside the 1954 Act renewal rights). Tell them the council, not you, confirms their rates.
say: "If this is the only unit your business uses, at a rateable value of £6,500 you may well pay no rates at all, but the council confirms that, so it's worth a quick call to them."
"Are you keeping your current unit? If so, the relief rules change, so let's check the figures before you commit."
ask: "Why are you moving, and when do you need to be in?"
"Will you keep your current premises, or hand them back?"
"What do you need inside: eaves height, a roller shutter, power, parking for vans?"
"How long a lease are you thinking of, and would you want a break clause?"
cards: Up to what rateable value is there no business rates to pay under small business rate relief?
£12,000 or less, if it is the only property the business uses.
Over what range does the relief taper from 100% to 0%?
Rateable values from £12,001 to £15,000.
How much relief does a rateable value of £13,500 get?
50% off the bill.
How long does main-property relief continue after taking a second property on or after 27 November 2025?
36 months (12 months if the second property was taken before that date).
What are the 2026/27 multipliers?
48p standard and 43.2p small business, for rateable values below £51,000.
